items.stem: What does vectorised arithmetic in R mean for x + y when x and y are numeric vectors?

options.text: The operation is applied element-wise across the vectors
options.rationale: R applies + to each aligned pair, a core idiom avoiding explicit loops.

options.text: Only the first elements are added
options.rationale: All aligned elements are combined, not just the first.

options.text: It raises an error unless lengths are equal
options.rationale: R recycles shorter vectors (with a warning if not a multiple), rather than always erroring.

items.explanation: R applies + to each aligned pair, a core idiom avoiding explicit loops.

items.stem: Select TWO correct statements about subsetting in R.

options.text: A logical vector can select elements where it is TRUE
options.rationale: Logical indexing keeps positions that are TRUE.

options.text: Negative indices drop the elements at those positions
options.rationale: Negative subscripts exclude elements in R.

options.text: df[df$x > 0] on a data frame filters rows like df[df$x > 0, ]
options.rationale: Single-bracket without a comma selects columns, not rows.

items.explanation: Logical indexing keeps positions that are TRUE.

items.stem: Why distinguish a factor from a character vector in R?

options.text: A factor stores a fixed set of levels and is treated as categorical in models and plots
options.rationale: Factors encode categories with levels, affecting modelling and plotting.

options.text: A factor can only hold numbers
options.rationale: Factors represent categories, often from text.

options.text: Characters cannot be stored in a data frame
options.rationale: Character vectors are perfectly valid columns.

options.text: Factors are always faster for arithmetic
options.rationale: Arithmetic on factors is generally inappropriate.

items.explanation: Factors encode categories with levels, affecting modelling and plotting.
